transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2027-03-21 16:00 UTC
- Duration: ~48 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Marco Diaz (CTO, Seabright), Leah Kim (Head of ML), Samir Patel (Infra)

Auto-summary (auto generated, brief): Seabright is evaluating Dedicated reserved GPUs for a low-latency search API with high burstiness and strict encryption needs. Key asks: isolation guarantees, burst handling, VPC+kms integration, and a benchmark plan.

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, AE at Redwood, with Priya who's our solution engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Marco: Hi Jordan, thanks. Doing good. Bit of a scavenger hunt this week but, uh, nice to meet you, Priya.
[00:12] Leah: Hi, thanks for setting this up. We wanted to walk through dedicated options — our infra and ML folks are both here to ask the hard questions.
[00:18] Priya: Great. Quick agenda — understand your workload shape, isolation and compliance needs, expected burst pattern, then we'll map to Dedicated and fallback options and propose a benchmark. Sound OK?
[00:26] Samir: Yep, that works. We'll be blunt — our traffic is spiky due to batch re-ranks and seasonal marketing pushes. We need predictable tail latency and no noisy neighbour problems.
[00:36] Jordan: Yep, that's exactly where Dedicated usually comes in. So quick question: are you leaning Private (VPC/on-prem) or Hosted with Dedicated reservation?
[00:45] Marco: We're still evaluating. Short-term we'd prefer Dedicated in a customer-isolated pool that sits in our VPC — so private plane-ish, and long term we may consider on-prem for cert stuff.
[00:55] Priya: Understood. Two immediate things to call out: 1) Dedicated reserved pools give you isolation and predictable throughput; 2) There are tradeoffs in handling sudden spikes — we have warm pool / pre-warm strategies and also a hosted fallback.
[01:06] Leah: Can you expand on the fallback? If we reserve N GPUs, what happens when we blow past that?
[01:10] Priya: Sure. Two modes: a) burst within your reserved capacity using hot/warm prewarmed nodes we keep on standby (billing depends on the reservation model) and b) overflow routing to hosted instances or compatible model-variants. Overflow keeps apps online but may incur higher latency and different data residency considerations.
[01:25] Samir: Residency is a big deal. We need all inference logs and payloads in our VPC and keys in our KMS. Any overflow to hosted — that could violate compliance.
[01:34] Jordan: Good flag. For strict residency you can use Redwood Private — that allows the control plane to remain customer-managed and ensures KMS/HSM stays with you. But Private has a longer lead time and different pricing.
[01:45] Marco: Lead time — how long are we talking? We have a Q2 compliance audit.
[01:49] Priya: Private on-prem or VPC installs generally take 6–10 weeks depending on access and the infra team's bandwidth. For dedicated reserved capacity in Redwood-hosted regions with VPC peering we can be quicker — often 2–3 weeks to provision the pool and set up peering and KMS.
[02:02] Leah: OK. For success criteria: we want p50 < 60ms for small embed calls and p95 < 300ms for our search re-rank pipeline at peak. Cost per 1M queries should be within our target (we gave a number in the intake form).
[02:16] Priya: Good specifics. We'll target those in the benchmark. Quick question on model footprint — are you running a quantized 7B open model for ranking and a heavier 13B for long-form generation?
[02:28] Marco: Exactly. 7B for live ranking, 13B for occasional generation. Rank is the latency-sensitive stuff.
[02:34] Samir: Also, our requests vary widely in sequence length. Many ranking calls are 64 tokens, generation can be 1k tokens but less frequent.
[02:42] Jordan: That matters for kernel selection and memory planning — KV cache size and sequence distribution will drive how many concurrent sessions a single GPU can handle.
[02:49] Priya: On that note, can you share your qps shape? Daily baseline and the spike multipliers?
[02:55] Leah: Baseline is around 150 qps sustained for rank traffic, but spikes land us at 2.5–3k qps for short bursts (2–10 minutes) during promotions.
[03:05] Samir: And we have scheduled batch operations that can cause long-running throughput too, like reindexing windows — those we can schedule, but they add sustained load for hours.
[03:14] Priya: OK so it's both short-duration microbursts and a few long windows. For short bursts we recommend a warm pool that can prewarm inference contexts — that reduces cold start latency and lets you absorb short surges. For longer windows you'd size reservations to cover baseline + planned events, or use autoscale policies with burst capacity if you accept slightly higher latency.
[03:33] Marco: What's the prewarm cost? We need to model economics.
[03:36] Jordan: Prewarm is charged as reserved compute (or as a reduced-rate standby) depending on the contract. We'll include explicit cost scenarios in the SKU doc. But practically it's often cheaper than paying for hosting overflow every spike.
[03:48] Leah: Also, we need strict audit logs and SSO (SAML) access for our engineers. Do dedicated deployments support token-level cost breakdowns and audit trails?
[03:58] Priya: Yes — Redwood Console provides token-level cost/latency breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and audit logs. For Private we can integrate with your SIEM and SAML. We'll capture the integrations in the security packet we share.
[04:11] Samir: About keys — we use an HSM-backed KMS (Cloud HSM). We need the model payload to be encrypted in transit and at rest and the keys never leave our control. Is that doable?
[04:22] Priya: Absolutely. We support KMS integrations and HSM policies. For Hosted with VPC peering we can use customer-managed KMS; for Private you have full control. We'll note the exact handshake and network requirements in the network appendix.
[04:34] Marco: Great. Could Priya walk through the benchmark plan you mentioned?
[04:38] Priya: Sure. Proposed: 1) Redwood provisions a 2-hour Dedicated test pool in your targeted region, with the same model binaries you run (7B quantized + 13B), 2) We'll replay a Seabright-supplied traffic trace scaled to 1x baseline and 10x spikes (you said 3k qps), 3) Capture p50/p95/p99 latency, GPU utilization, token cost, and fallbacks triggered, 4) We'll run two variants: with warm-pool prewarm on and off to show delta.
[05:05] Leah: We'll need to scrub the traffic trace for PII before sharing.
[05:09] Priya: Yep, totally expected — anonymized traces are fine. We'll also provide a small synthetic harness so you can reproduce the test yourself.
[05:16] Samir: During the test, if we route overflow to hosted, does the payload leave our VPC? That'll be a blocker for us.
[05:23] Priya: If overflow routing is to Redwood-hosted without peering, it would. For the benchmark we can limit overflow to measure theoretical capacity but keep traffic internal — or use Private staging to ensure no egress. We can mirror both options.
[05:36] Jordan: Quick aside — one pattern we see: customers reserve for baseline + keep a small warm pool and allow a controlled fraction of overflow for absolute peaks, plus burst-fallback SLAs. It reduces cost while keeping availability.
[05:48] Marco: Sounds sensible. One other wrinkle — we use per-tenant quotas and some tenants are higher priority. Can Redwood support tenant-level prioritization within a Dedicated pool?
[05:58] Priya: Yes — you can map routing policies to prioritize traffic buckets or tokens. Within a reserved pool we can enforce soft quotas and preempt lower-priority work during contention. We'll share config examples.
[06:10] Leah: How does quantization impact memory and throughput in these scenarios? We saw conflicting numbers in benchmark reports.
[06:16] Priya: Quantization reduces memory footprint and increases throughput in many cases, but it depends on kernel availability. For 7B quantized, you typically get 2–3x more concurrency per GPU. For 13B it's model-dependent; we recommend running the precise binary in the benchmark so the numbers reflect your payload.
[06:33] Samir: On networking, we need to avoid hairpin egress and want strict ACLs. We'll share the VPC CIDR ranges and preferred peering pattern. Anything we should know about the peering?
[06:43] Jordan: We'll need an AWS account role for peering setup, some firewall rules for the control plane, and maybe a temporary rule to run the benchmark agent. We'll detail those steps in the network appendix.
[06:54] Marco: Timeline-wise, if we sign a PO in early April, can we get a bench and go-live by late May?
[07:01] Priya: That timeline is plausible for Redwood-hosted Dedicated + VPC peering. Private on-prem would push later. We'll include an expected timeline in the proposal.
[07:10] Leah: A couple of nitty-gritty items — we need to know behavior under NVidia preemption (if we use spot-like instances) and how warm-pool interacts.
[07:20] Priya: Dedicated reservations use preemptible options only if you opt for lower cost. For strict SLOs you pick non-preemptible reserved nodes. Warm pool nodes are held warm and not preempted unless you opt in.
[07:31] Samir: We care about telemetry — does Redwood export GPU-level metrics to Prometheus or Datadog?
[07:37] Priya: Yes, we can integrate with both and push per-node and per-request metrics; token-level traces are available through the console and via export hooks.
[07:46] Jordan: Let's talk cost modeling briefly. Leah, you mentioned a target cost per 1M queries. We'll produce three scenarios: baseline reserved to meet p95 targets, baseline+warm-pool vs baseline+overflow to hosted. That'll show unit economics.
[08:00] Leah: Perfect. Also, can we run a short functional test of RBAC and SAML before the full bench? We want to make sure engineers can access logs.
[08:07] Priya: Absolutely — our onboarding includes a security/SSO smoke test. We'll schedule that with your infra lead.
[08:13] Marco: Any customer references who did this exact stack? Preferably in fintech or analytics.
[08:18] Jordan: We can share a redacted case study — a fintech customer used a similar pattern: reserved baseline, warm pool for bursts, private KMS, and a hosted fallback for exceptional peaks. We'll send the case study with the proposal.
[08:29] Samir: About SLA — what latency/uptime SLAs apply to Dedicated pools?
[08:34] Priya: SLA is uptime-based for Dedicated pools; latency SLOs are customer-configurable but not SLA-backed unless in an enterprise plan. We can discuss enterprise ramping if low-latency SLA is required.
[08:47] Leah: For the benchmark's success criteria, besides p50/p95/p99, we want the cost per token and per-request breakdown and the amount of overflow triggered during 10x spikes.
[08:58] Priya: Noted — we'll capture token counts, GPU utilization, and the delta with/without warm pool.
[09:05] Marco: Anything else on our side to share now?
[09:09] Samir: I'll export an anonymized traffic trace, VPC CIDRs, and our KMS spec. Expect those by Thursday.
[09:16] Leah: We'll also attach our priority tenant list and current qps per tenant so you can test prioritization.
[09:21] Jordan: Great. I'll follow up with the pricing doc and the benchmark test plan. Priya will reach out to schedule the test window.
[09:29] Marco: One final question — what about model variant fallbacks? If the quantized 7B runs into a memory wall, can you automatically route to a slightly different model configuration?
[09:38] Priya: Yes — smart routing policies can fallback to a compatible variant (e.g., lower sequence length, smaller quantized binary) to keep latency within reason. We'll demo that in the benchmark if you want.
[09:49] Leah: We'd like that — please show how routing rules affect p95 during the test.
[09:53] Jordan: Cool. Let's recap next steps — Jordan sends pricing and case study, Priya schedules and runs the 2-hour bench with warm-pool on/off, Seabright shares traces and VPC/KMS info, Samir will confirm peering windows.
[10:10] Marco: Great meeting. Thanks, everyone.
[10:13] Jordan: Thanks all, we'll follow up in email.

End of transcript.
